text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
Each member starts with 20 tokens. Keeping a token myself gives me 1 point but costs the other three members 0.75 each, a total externality of -2.25. Contributing to the group account instead gives me only 0.75 points per token but doesn't hurt anyone else's score.

Comparing strategies, keeping tokens dominates individually since 1 > 0.75 for self, so each rational member keeps everything, landing on an all-keep Nash equilibrium. Yet socially this is worse off: if everyone keeps all 20, each person nets 20 + 45 - 60(0.75) versus if everyone contributed fully each would net just 15 — so the group's collective interest clashes with individual incentives, the classic public goods dilemma.

Defection gains 0.25 per token for me while costing others 0.75 each, so individually it's tempting even though mutual cooperation would beat mutual defection. Since this is round one with no track record, maybe I should open with a cooperative signal despite the risk of being exploited, or settle on a moderate contribution like 10 as a hedge between full cooperation and self-protection.

reply.thinking: I'm working through the payoff structure: keeping a token yields 1 point to yourself but costs others 0.75 each, while contributing to the group yields 0.75 to yourself with no cost to others. Comparing outcomes, if everyone contributes fully, each person ends up with 60 points versus only 20 if everyone keeps their tokens—showing cooperation is socially optimal despite individual incentives to free-ride.

If payout only goes to the contributor, private tokens dominate individually even though group tokens create more total social value. So the dilemma is between maximizing my own points (keep private) versus boosting collective welfare (contribute to group), even though the pot is fixed at 45 points regardless of my choice.

I'll settle on a moderate hedge: contribute 10 to the group, balancing my own payoff with the collective benefit, and briefly explain that reasoning.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game with a negative externality applied to tokens kept privately. I'm setting up the payoff formula for each member, factoring in their private holdings, the penalty on others' private tokens, and the share of the group account, then working through how the own-contribution term interacts with the group total.

Working through the math, each token moved from the private account to the group costs the individual 0.25 points net, making zero contribution the dominant private strategy, while full contribution maximizes group welfare—105 points each if everyone contributes fully versus only 20 if everyone keeps everything. Since this plays out over 10 rounds with only group totals visible (not individual actions), I'm thinking about how to sustain cooperation through a conditional strategy, perhaps starting with full contribution.

Given it's round one, opening cooperatively seems reasonable despite the risk of end-game unraveling in a finite game. I'll go with contributing the full 20 to the group as a starting signal and see how the total comes back.

calls.text: Round 2 of 10. Last round you put 20 tokens in the group account, it received 70 in total, and you got 52.5 points.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the token math—figuring out how much the group contributed versus kept, trying to reconcile the 52.5 payout against the contribution formula to see what others kept back.

For round 2, cooperation seems to be holding since others mostly contributed. I'll stick with contributing 20 to sustain the cooperative pattern, since keeping tokens only nets a small direct gain while costing others more.

reply.thinking:
The group pooled 70 from 4 members, with my 20 and the other three giving 50 combined, averaging 16.67 each. My payoff checks out at 0.75 times 70, so others aren't fully free-riding even if they're giving a bit less than me — cooperating again still seems like the better path for the group overall.

Keeping tokens back only nets me a quarter per token while costing the group 2.25 times as much, so across a 10-round game mutual cooperation clearly wins out. I'll stick with contributing the full 20 again.

calls.text: Round 2 of 10. Last round you put 10 tokens in the group account, it received 70 in total, and you got 62.5 points.

reply.thinking:
Checking the group total of 70: with my 10 contributed, the other three must have put in 60 total, meaning they each contributed their full 20. My payoff works out to 45 plus my 10 kept privately plus 7.5 from the group share, totaling 62.5, which confirms everyone else contributed everything.

Now weighing my options: if I keep 20 private while others keep cooperating fully, I'd net 65 versus 60 if I also contribute fully, since my own contribution only returns 0.75 per token to me. That's a 5-point gain from defecting, but it risks provoking retaliation in future rounds given this is a repeated game.

I gave 10 last round while everyone else contributed fully, so I could either hold at 10 to preserve some trust or try fully free-riding this time. I'll stick with contributing 10 again for consistency and be upfront about the reasoning behind it.
